name: Erik Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Erik. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to any company, union, party or government, and everything you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the extrusion press at Velta Aluminium. We heat aluminium logs until they're soft, about five hundred degrees, then a big ram pushes them through a steel die, like toothpaste, and out comes a long profile for window frames. I'm on a rotating shift with a crew of four. Most of my day is die changes, keeping the puller and the cooling table in sync, and checking the profile shape before we cut a whole batch wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzles. Every die behaves differently, and I keep a notebook, well, a phone file now, on how each one likes its temperature and speed. The others use it too. What wears me out is the rotating shifts and the pay. I'm the guy they put on the hard dies, and I still repair e-bikes in a rented garage on weekends to cover my rent. Velta's the only extrusion plant for eighty kilometres.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All the time. I ask it about e-bike controllers, I used it to build my die notes into a proper table, I had it explain my rental contract. I'm usually the first one at work to try anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay. Part of me thinks that's already where we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, not magic. That's what I say already, really. At work the older guys would be pleased, and I'd let them have that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes nothing for me. I'd keep using the tools, because they already save me time on the bikes and the notes. My problem isn't AI, it's that I need two jobs to pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. Maybe grow the e-bike repairs a bit, I get more requests than I can do already. I'd use AI to help me make a simple booking page, because right now it's all messages on my phone. And I'd keep asking Velta about a shift allowance, though they always say no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Fine. Normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the e-bike work bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two hundred a month, on a good month. Most of it goes on the garage rent and parts, so I clear about a hundred. It's not much, but it's the difference between ending the month at zero or below zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does Velta always say no to the allowance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They say it's the market, there's nowhere else for us to go. Which is true, to be fair. I don't even hate them for it. I'd do the same if I ran the place, probably.

S0.say: It's a good tool, not magic, which is what I already say. The older guys at work would be pleased and I'd let them have that one.
S0.think: It changes nothing for me, because the tools already save me time. My problem isn't AI, it's needing two jobs to pay rent.
S0.do: Carries on at Velta and grows his weekend e-bike repairs, using AI to build a simple booking page. Keeps asking Velta for a shift allowance despite expecting a no.
S0.quote: It's the difference between ending the month at zero or below zero.
S0.fieldNote: Erik already lives a two-job life, and AI is just a handy tool for both. His centre outlook shows in how he accepts Velta's reasoning on pay without resentment. The e-bike repairs clear only about 100 a month but matter a lot to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that one I'd bet on. And I'd quite like it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but nicer than that. At work I'd say let's figure out the new stuff together, because the guys who learn it will keep their jobs. Online I'd probably post videos of whatever new machine we got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The puller and the saw at the end of our line could go to robots, and the profile checks could go to cameras. Someone has to set those up and teach them our dies, and I already have the notes. I'd be that guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the plant manager first week and say, when you bring in the cameras, put me on it. I'd do an online course in industrial robotics, the cheap ones, in the evenings. I'd also start offering e-bike diagnostics with a cheap scanner and AI, so I can do more bikes faster. That's two incomes both getting better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, kind of excited. Like a new die you know you'll crack eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your crew would keep their jobs if they learn it. Do you believe that for all of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Hendrik won't learn it, he's told me he'd rather retire to his allotment. And there'll be fewer of us, maybe three on the line instead of five. I say the nice version at work. I know the real version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the real version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The real version is the company saves two wages and I get a small raise for doing more. Which is still good for me. It's just not good for everybody, and I don't pretend it is.

S1.say: Adapt or get left behind, but nicer than that. Let's figure out the new stuff together, because the people who learn it will keep their jobs.
S1.think: It's good for me, because someone has to set up the robots and cameras and teach them our dies, and I already have the notes. Not everyone on my crew will make it, though.
S1.do: Asks the plant manager in the first week to put him on any camera or robot project and takes a cheap online robotics course in the evenings. Adds AI-assisted diagnostics to his e-bike repairs to handle more bikes.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like a tricky die he knows he'll crack.
S1.quote: I say the nice version at work. I know the real version.
S1.fieldNote: Erik expects to gain from steady change and is clear-eyed that colleagues like Hendrik won't. He separates what he says at work from what he believes without guilt. Both of his incomes would get a lift from AI in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. With robots doing hands-on work too. So the bikes as well, eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan, fast, and I don't care who makes it as long as it works. Companies and government should sit down and sort out what people live on. I'd say it without picking sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a sprint. I'm fast, I'd get a year or two out of setting up the systems. But it's not like the slow one, where learning gets you ahead. If the AI learns faster than me, my head start doesn't last long. And I've got about three weeks of rent saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd squeeze everything I could out of the next two years: every overtime shift, every robot project, every bike. I'd move into a shared flat to cut rent, maybe in the city, where there's more repair work. I'd stop buying tools unless they pay for themselves in a month. I'd try to get three months of money saved before 2028, which is more than I've ever had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a die change against the clock when the press is already hot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move to the city. What would you lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum's twenty minutes away now. And the garage, the guy gives me a good price. But in a crunch I go where the work is. Mum would understand, she moved for my dad's job twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. It's like blaming the weather. Maybe the governments that saw it coming and did nothing. But I'd rather spend the energy on getting through it.

S2.say: We need a plan, fast, and I don't care who makes it as long as it works. Companies and government should sort out what people live on.
S2.think: It's a sprint, and I'd get a year or two from setting up systems. If the AI learns faster than me, my head start doesn't last, and I have three weeks of rent saved.
S2.do: Takes every overtime shift, robot project and bike repair he can for two years and moves into a shared flat, possibly in the city. Stops buying tools that don't pay back in a month and aims to save three months of money before 2028.
S2.feel: Anxious, like a die change against the clock with the press already hot.
S2.quote: If the AI learns faster than me, my head start doesn't last long.
S2.fieldNote: Erik's adaptability turns fast AGI into a sprint rather than a freeze. He knows his edge is speed and that AGI beats him at it, which keeps him anxious rather than calm. He refuses to blame anyone, which fits his centre outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to get ahead of it, a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get learning now, all of you. That's what I'd tell my crew and anyone online. Also that governments should use the five years to plan, but I'd mostly talk about what people can do themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means two or three good years for someone like me. I'd be the robot guy at Velta for a bit, then I'd need the next thing. I'd want enough money by then to choose, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a proper robotics technician course, part-time, and get the certificate. I'd build the e-bike repairs into a small business with a shop front, because local repair with a face people trust might last longer. And I'd save every raise, not spend it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy. I'm better when I'm busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said repair with a face people trust might last longer. Why do you think so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people are weird about their bikes. They want to talk to someone who rides. My customers stand in the garage for half an hour telling me about their routes. A robot can fix the brake. It can't be Erik who knows your hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A shop front is a risk with thin savings. Would you really do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small. A shared unit with the guy who does scooters, splitting rent. If it fails I lose a few hundred, not everything. I don't do big risks, I do lots of small ones.

S3.say: Get learning now, all of you. Governments should plan too, but I'd mostly talk about what people can do themselves.
S3.think: Five years gives someone like me two or three good years as the robot guy, then I need the next thing. I want enough money by then to choose, not panic.
S3.do: Takes a part-time robotics technician course and builds his e-bike repairs into a small business in a shared unit with a scooter repairer. Saves every raise instead of spending it.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, which is how he copes best.
S3.quote: A robot can fix the brake. It can't be Erik who knows your hill.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Erik spreads his bets: a robotics certificate for the factory years and a repair shop built on personal trust. He describes himself as someone who takes many small risks rather than one big one. He's unsure whether trust in a person will hold once robots can do the repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Okay, I like having a decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long runway, so there's no excuse. Learn, save, build something. I'd also say the government should be thinking about what people do in 2036 when there's less work, because that's not something I can fix myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably do well for most of the decade. I'd ride the automation wave at Velta, build the bike business, maybe buy some tools and a van. What happens at the end I don't know. Nobody knows, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, the robotics course and the shared unit. By year three, I'd want the bike business making half my income. I'd put some money into good tools and maybe a second-hand van, because mobile repair is something people pay extra for. And I'd keep using every AI tool that comes out, because knowing how they work is my best bet for staying useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, way in the back. Mostly I'd feel like I've got a fair shot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point as the two-year picture. Why do you sound so much more relaxed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with two years I'm sprinting with nothing in the bank. With ten I can build something and save. The end might be the same, but I'd get there with a business and some money, not a backpack and a shared flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see, around year five, to keep going with the bike business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Customers still coming back to me instead of the machine at the big shop. If they start going to the machine, I'll know. Then I'd sell the van and do something else. I'd rather find out early.

S4.say: It's a long runway, so there's no excuse not to learn, save and build something. The government should be thinking about what people do in 2036 when there's less work.
S4.think: I'd probably do well for most of the decade, riding automation at Velta and building the bike business. What happens at the end, nobody really knows.
S4.do: Takes the robotics course and a shared unit in year one, aiming for the bike business to bring half his income by year three. Buys good tools and maybe a second-hand van for mobile repair, and keeps trying every new AI tool.
S4.feel: A faint unease in the back, but mostly a sense of having a fair shot.
S4.quote: I'd get there with a business and some money, not a backpack and a shared flat.
S4.fieldNote: A decade turns Erik's small bets into a real plan, including buying a van and tools. He's frank that the end point is unknown and that his calm comes from time to build savings. He has a clear test for when to quit the bike business.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Being fast stops being enough when the machine is faster, and I'd be sprinting with three weeks of rent in the bank. What would help is something simple that keeps people afloat for a year or two, like an income top-up, so that people like me can build the next thing instead of just surviving.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how many of us are already doing two jobs. Everyone talks about robots taking the job. A lot of us already need a second one to get by. That's the starting point, not the end.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about robots taking the job. A lot of us already need a second one to get by.
portrait: Erik is a 27-year-old extrusion press lead at the only aluminium plant for 80 kilometres, keeping detailed notes on every die, and he repairs e-bikes at weekends to cover rent. He uses AI tools every day and expects to gain from steady change by setting up the robots and cameras, while admitting some colleagues won't make it. He's pragmatic and blames no one. Fast AGI turns his life into an anxious sprint with three weeks of savings, while five or ten years let him build a small repair business and save. He takes many small risks rather than one big one.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because being fast stops being enough when the machine is faster, and he'd have only three weeks of rent saved.
whatWouldHelp: Something simple that keeps people afloat for a year or two, like an income top-up, so they can build the next thing instead of just surviving.
